title: The CPU: fetch, decode, execute
task: Write `run(memory, max_steps=1000)` for the 8-instruction machine in the table. Copy the memory, then loop: fetch `mem[pc]`, advance `pc` (wrapping at 32), decode the opcode (top 3 bits) and address (low 5 bits), and execute. Stop on `HALT` or after `max_steps`. Return `{"acc", "pc", "memory", "halted", "steps"}`.
hints: Set up `mem = list(memory)`, `acc = pc = steps = 0` and `halted = False`. Loop `while steps < max_steps:`. Inside, fetch with `word = mem[pc]`, then `pc = (pc + 1) % 32` and `steps += 1`.

Decode with `op, addr = word >> 5, word & 31`. Then use an if/elif chain: `if op == 0: halted = True; break`, `elif op == 1: acc = mem[addr]`, `elif op == 3: acc = (acc + mem[addr]) % 256`, and so on.

The jumps: `elif op == 5: pc = addr`, `elif op == 6 and acc == 0: pc = addr`, and `elif op == 7 and acc >= 128: pc = addr`. At the end, `return {"acc": acc, "pc": pc, "memory": mem, "halted": halted, "steps": steps}`.

options.why: The top 3 bits are 110 = 6, which is JZ. The low 5 bits are 01000 = 8. Check: 6 × 32 + 8 = 200.
JMP is opcode 5 (101). The top three bits here are 110, which is 6.
The address field is only 5 bits, so it maxes out at 31. Split the word: 3 bits of opcode, 5 bits of address.

quiz.q: Why does the CPU advance `pc` before executing the instruction?

options.text: So a jump can just overwrite pc, and every other instruction moves on to the next one for free
options.why: After the fetch, pc already points at the next instruction. A jump replaces that, and everything else leaves it alone.
The order is about control flow, not speed.

options.text: It doesn't matter: either order gives the same result
options.why: If you advance after executing, a jump's new pc gets bumped by one and lands on the wrong instruction.
